summary: Shafik Quoraishee introduces his independent research applying AI and NLP to the NYT Connections game, clarifying it is not internal NYT research and results are preliminary. Connections, launched in 2023 and edited by Wyna Liu, became the Times' second most played game after Wordle, with hundreds of millions of plays in its first year. The game presents 16 words to be grouped into four categories of four, with difficulty tiers from yellow to purple, the latter notorious for decoy overlaps and polysemous words. The talk covers system 1 versus system 2 thinking, combinatorics of random guessing, and models the game as an augmented graph coloring problem where words are vertices, categories are colors, and edges encode relationship strength. Semantic similarity alone is insufficient; relationships span orthographic, morphological, encyclopedic, and associative types, with polysemous words posing the greatest challenge. Relational alignment metrics, visualized via heat maps, can computationally distinguish easy from hard puzzles, with solve rates of roughly 19% for hard puzzles versus 70%+ for easier ones. Quoraishee extends this to multi-dimensional analysis: words can relate in multiple ways simultaneously, requiring radar charts and multi-dimensional hypergraphs that capture inter- and intra-cluster strengths across semantic categories. A semantic distribution evaluation framework tracks categorical distributions (hypernymy, morphology, orthography) over time. Semantic graphs are constructed using lexical databases like WordNet and ConceptNet plus word embeddings. The primary solver is a graph convolutional neural network (GNN) that outputs candidate subgraphs, paired with a reinforcement learning system that optimizes edge and node weights to navigate cluster morphology. This two-part system shows somewhat reasonable improvement in solvability for a small subset of hard puzzles. Quoraishee raises concerns that LLMs may pull puzzle solutions from internet training data and remain black boxes, motivating connection to the ArcGI benchmark. Next steps include extending evaluation to more puzzles and exploring game development applications.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Caveats
sections.summary: Quoraishee introduces himself as a NYT Games developer with ML, mobile, and data science background. He clarifies this is independent, preliminary, investigatory research separate from internal NYT research, inspired by but not based on third-party work.

sections.title: Introduction to Connections
sections.summary: Explains Connections: launched June 2023 beta, August 2023 official, edited by Wyna Liu, second to Wordle in popularity. Players group 16 words into four categories of four, with up to four wrong guesses. Difficulty tiers are yellow, green, blue, and purple, with purple featuring decoy overlaps. All puzzles and mechanics are and will remain human-made.

sections.title: Why Connections is Interesting for AI
sections.summary: The game challenges AI abstract reasoning, tests avoidance of overfitting and superficial similarities, requires clean explainable solutions, and offers a reproducible benchmark due to fixed inputs. Shows ChatGPT 4o giving a wrong solution as an example.

sections.title: Human vs. AI Problem Solving
sections.summary: Discusses system 1 (fast intuitive) vs. system 2 (slow deliberate) thinking from Kahneman. Effective players use both. Canonical failures occur in both modes. Third-party benchmarks show progressive LLM capability but imperfect solve rates with caveats.

sections.title: AI Analysis and Methodology
sections.summary: Presents combinatorics: near 0% random win from full board, 1 in 5,000-6,000 after one category, 1 in 35 after two. Models Connections as augmented graph coloring: words as vertices, categories as colors, edges as connection strength, creating the search space for algorithms.

sections.title: Semantic Similarity
sections.summary: Argues semantic similarity is not all you need. Distinguishes relationship types: orthographic (anagrams), morphological (shared suffixes), encyclopedic (newspaper category), and associative (colors). Polysemous words like 'mole' are hardest for both AI and humans.

sections.title: Relational Alignment
sections.summary: Introduces relational alignment as a metric associating word pairs, with a heat map simulation comparing metrics. Claims relational alignment can computationally distinguish easy from hard puzzles, showing examples of each.

sections.title: Multi-dimensional Analysis
sections.summary: Expands relational alignment to multi-dimensional analysis: words relate in multiple ways with different scores across categories, visualized via radar charts. A semantic distribution evaluation framework tracks categorical distributions (hypernymy, morphology, orthography) over time. Graph coloring extends to graph clustering with multi-dimensional hypergraphs capturing inter- and intra-cluster strengths. Semantic graphs are built using WordNet, ConceptNet, and word embeddings, increasing the intelligence space procedurally for explainable AI.

sections.title: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs)
sections.summary: The primary solver is a graph convolutional neural network that takes a graph as input and outputs candidate subgraphs as potential solutions. This is part of a two-part system paired with reinforcement learning, which optimizes edge and node weights and tracks cluster morphology. A system diagram combines RL agents with the GNN. Three-space visualization shows semantic graph candidates with RL-guided traversal. Solvability rate for a small subset of hard puzzles increases somewhat reasonably, though work is in progress.

sections.title: Motivation and Next Steps
sections.summary: Motivates the approach over LLMs: LLMs are trained on internet data where puzzle solutions are available, creating contamination concerns, and their solutions remain black boxes. Next steps include connecting to the ArcGI benchmark, extending the approach to more puzzles, and exploring game development applications.
